title: Correlative Conjunctions
keyIdea: Correlative conjunctions are pairs of joining words that work together: either … or, neither … nor, both … and, not only … but also, and whether … or. Each pair has its own meaning: either … or picks one of two, neither … nor rules out both, both … and takes the two together. The words after each half must match in kind (parallel structure): "both swimming and running", not "both swimming and to run". With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "Neither the players nor the coach was ready." With both … and, the verb is plural.
familyTip: Play "neither, nor" at dinner: your child says what they will not eat, using neither … nor (neither sprouts nor olives). Then switch to both … and and either … or. Listen for the classic slip, neither … or, and for halves that do not match, like either walk or by bus.

visual.caption: Correct or needs fixing? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Both cats and dogs make good pets.
She is not only kind but also funny.
You can either walk or by bus.
Either my sisters or my brother is here.
Both the cake and the jam was gone.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match each first word to its partner, pick the pair for the meaning, balance both halves, choose the verb, and drag the first word into place.

kid: Some joining words come in pairs. Either goes with or. Neither goes with nor. Both goes with and. Not only goes with but also. Whether goes with or.
Each pair means something. Either Sam or Priya can come: just one of them. Neither Sam nor Priya can come: not one of them. Both Sam and Priya can come: the two of them.
The two halves must match. She likes both swimming and running. Swimming and running are the same kind of word. She likes both swimming and to run does not match.
With either or neither, look at the person nearest the verb. Neither the players nor the coach was ready. The coach is one person, so we say was. With both, there are always two, so we say were.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. This is Common Core L.5.1e: use correlative conjunctions (either/or, neither/nor). In England, Key Stage 2 pupils learn to use conjunctions to express time, cause and contrast and to build cohesion, and correlative pairs extend that work. The pairs are either … or, neither … nor, both … and, not only … but also, and whether … or.

Each pair carries meaning: either … or offers alternatives (one of two), neither … nor negates both, both … and adds the two together, not only … but also adds the second as extra or surprising, and whether … or presents alternatives under doubt or choice. What follows the first word and what follows the second should be grammatically parallel: two nouns, two verbs, two adjectives, or two phrases of the same kind.

Agreement follows the proximity rule in standard usage: with either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Either my sisters or my brother is coming; Either my brother or my sisters are coming). Subjects joined by both … and are plural.

Common mistakes: neither … or instead of neither … nor; unbalanced halves (either walk or by bus); placing the first word too early so the halves no longer match (I either will phone you or text you); and making the verb agree with the first subject (Neither the players nor the coach were ready). In the lab your child matches five pairs, chooses pairs by meaning, balances four sentences, fixes four verbs, and drags the first word into place.

practice.explain: Neither pairs with nor: neither tea nor coffee. Neither … or is a common slip.

practice.prompt: "Neither the girl nor the {n} boys ___ here." The verb agrees with how many people?
practice.hint: Look at the subject nearer the verb.
practice.explain: The nearer subject is the {n} boys, so the verb agrees with {n} people and is plural: were.

choices: We can either walk or take the bus.
We can either walk or by bus.
We can either walk or walking.
practice.hint: What comes after either? What comes after or? Do they match?
practice.explain: Walk and take the bus are both actions after can, so the halves match. By bus has no action word, and walking is a different form.

practice.prompt: "Both the {a} cats and the {b} dogs ___ hungry." How many animals is the verb about?
practice.hint: Both … and adds the two groups together.
practice.explain: Both … and adds them: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} animals, so the verb is plural: are.

practice.prompt: Choose the verb: "Either my aunts or my uncle ___ coming."
practice.hint: Which subject is nearer to the verb?
practice.explain: The nearer subject is my uncle, one person, so is. If it were Either my uncle or my aunts, it would be are.

pool.explain: Not only pairs with but also: not only fast but also careful.

pool.prompt: Which pair fits? "We can visit ___ on Saturday ___ on Sunday, but not both."
pool.hint: The sentence says we pick one day.
pool.explain: Either … or means one of the two. Both … and would mean both days, and neither … nor would mean no day.

choices: Neither Ali nor Ben was late.
Neither Ali or Ben was late.
Neither Ali nor Ben were late.
pool.hint: Check the partner word, then the verb.
pool.explain: Neither pairs with nor, and the nearer subject is Ben, one person, so was.

choices: He is both clever and kind.
He is both clever and has kindness.
He both is clever and kind.
pool.hint: Clever is a describing word. What should come after and?
pool.explain: Clever and kind are both describing words. Has kindness does not match, and both before is makes the halves uneven.

pool.prompt: Where should either go? "I will phone you or text you."
pool.hint: Put it just before the first of the two matching parts.
pool.explain: I will either phone you or text you. Now phone you and text you match.

pool.prompt: "Either the {n} players or the coach ___ to blame." The verb agrees with how many people?
pool.hint: Look at the subject nearer the verb, not the first one.
pool.explain: The nearer subject is the coach, so the verb agrees with 1 person, not {n}: is.

pool.prompt: A paragraph uses {n} correlative pairs, and every pair is either … or. How many joining words is that?
pool.hint: Each pair has two words: either and or.
pool.explain: Each pair is 2 words, so {n} pairs make {=2*n} joining words.

pool.prompt: Which pair fits? "I can't decide ___ to read ___ to draw."
pool.hint: The sentence is about a choice still to be made.
pool.explain: Whether … or presents a choice that is still undecided.

pool.prompt: Choose the verb: "Both the bread and the milk ___ fresh."
pool.hint: How many things does both … and join?
pool.explain: Both … and joins two things, so the verb is plural: are.
